1:
With the enemies' appeal lodged against them, the fate of the temple now hangs on a search through the imperial archives, and the witnesses gather around the decree Darius issued and the record-house it sent his officers hunting through. The reformed John Gill reads the order simply: Darius commanded inquiry to be made after the edict of Cyrus, that the public records be searched for it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the place — search was made in the house of the books, where the treasures were also laid up, at Babylon, since it was there that Cyrus had been when he signed it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers on the phrase itself: the 'house of the rolls' is the house of the books, the king's library, and he marks it as the first mention of a library in all of Scripture.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the archival errand into a drama of providence. The Samaritans had appealed to Cyrus's decree because the Jews pleaded it, perhaps hoping it would never be found, so that their plea might be over-ruled and the work stopped; for the tribes, he notes, had not taken care to provide themselves with an authentic copy that might have served them, but were forced to appeal to the original. When it was not found at Babylon, Darius did not seize on the failure as a pretext to conclude that no such decree existed and give judgment against the Jews. Perhaps, Henry suggests, some who durst not destroy the roll had hidden it out of ill will, that the Jews might lose its benefit; but Providence so ordered that it came to light.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, corrects the rendering: 'made a decree' is rather 'gave an order,' and 'were laid up' is in the original 'laid down,' in a chamber for the storing of documents and other treasures. John Wesley agrees on the sequence — search was first made in Babylon, and only when the edict was not found there did they search at Achmetha, and find it.

Henry draws the governing lesson the chapter will unfold: the heart of kings is in the hand of God, who turns it whichever way he pleases, for he is King of kings; and what is intended for the prejudice of the church is often, by his overruling providence, made serviceable to it, so that out of the eater comes forth meat — the very appeal meant to suppress the Jews will instead procure them supply, as Philippians 1:12 teaches that the things which happened fell out rather to the furtherance of the gospel.
2:
The discovery of the roll at Achmetha rather than Babylon sets the witnesses to work on the geography, and they converge, against an old misreading, on a single identification. The reformed John Gill first clears away the error of Jarchi and Aben Ezra, who took Achmetha to be the name of a vessel or chest in which writings were stored for safety; it was, beyond doubt, a place — the Ecbatana of the Vulgate and of Josephus, a city in Media whose very name is drawn from heat. There the kings of Persia kept their summer residence, dwelling at Shushan in the winter and at Ecbatana in the summer, so that Aelian likens them to cranes, birds of passage shuttling between their seasons.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain why the search had to travel so far. In Babylon itself the document was not found; but the search there probably turned up a note that papers from the time of Cyrus were preserved in the fortress of Achmetha, where the record was at length discovered. Achmetha, they add, was the capital of Great Media, the Ecbatana built by Dejokes, summer seat of the Persian and Parthian kings, near the modern Hamadan, the form of the name preserving an Old-Median or Old-Persian pronunciation; and its citadel would have housed the royal palace and the official buildings where such archives lay.

Charles Ellicott offers a shrewd conjecture about why Babylon failed to yield the roll: the original parchment, he suggests, had probably been destroyed at Babylon by the usurper Smerdis, so that what was found at Ecbatana was a copy, likely a Chaldean transcript. Adam Clarke agrees that Ecbatana was the summer residence of the Persian kings and supposes the records of Cyrus had been carried thither; John Wesley names it simply the royal city of the Medes and Persians.

The witnesses do not divide. Together they turn a dry note of provenance into a quiet testimony of providence: the decree that the Jews' adversaries hoped had perished, or could not be produced, was preserved in a mountain fortress far from where it was signed, and the God who moves the hearts of kings had seen to it that a summer palace in Media should keep safe the one document on which the rebuilding of his house now turned. What man had mislaid, or perhaps concealed, the ordering of heaven brought forth at the appointed hour.
3:
The recovered edict opens with its warrant — 'let the house be builded, the place where they offered sacrifices' — and the witnesses attend chiefly to the strange dimensions it prescribes and to the pledge of royal support. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the decree in full: in the first year of Cyrus the king made his order concerning the house of God at Jerusalem, that it be built as a place of sacrifice, its foundations strongly laid, its height threescore cubits and its breadth threescore cubits. Charles Ellicott hears behind 'strongly laid' the prophetic word of Isaiah 44:28, 'thy foundation shall be laid,' and notes that the decree adds a term signifying a sufficient and solid support.

The great puzzle is the measurement, for these proportions do not match Solomon's temple, and the two remaining witnesses take different roads to resolve it. Adam Clarke simply registers the fact: this was much larger than the first house, sixty cubits high and sixty broad, where Solomon's had been but thirty high and twenty broad. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley is unwilling to leave the discrepancy bare and proposes two ways to reconcile it. Either Solomon's cubits were the sacred cubit, larger than the common measure used here; or else the sixty cubits of height are meant only of the porch, as the porch of the first temple rose to a hundred and twenty. He adds a nicety of translation: the word rendered 'breadth' may as well mean the extension or length of the building, since it would be strange for the king to legislate the breadth and say nothing of the length.

So the schools part company gently over the arithmetic — Clarke content that the second temple was ordered on a grander scale, Wesley harmonizing the figures by the sacred cubit or by referring the height to the porch alone. Neither treats the difference as more than a problem of measurement; both agree the decree is genuine and generous.

Beneath the numbers the witnesses see one thing plainly. A pagan emperor has taken it upon himself to specify the dimensions and the fabric of the God of Israel's sanctuary, and to name it 'the place where they offered sacrifices' — acknowledging, in the very language of his decree, that this was no ordinary building but a house for the worship of heaven. The God who had moved Cyrus to release the captives now stands behind the record that will compel a later king to honour the same word, so that even the cubits of the temple were, in a manner, underwritten by the throne of Persia at the prompting of a higher throne.
4:
The specification of materials — 'three rows of great stones, and a row of new timber' — and the promise that 'the expences be given out of the king's house' draw the witnesses into the practical mechanics of the building and the vexed question of who actually paid for it. The reformed John Gill reports the reading of Jarchi, who understood the three rows of the walls, and took the great stones to be marble. Adam Clarke describes the technique, which he says the reader has met before: three courses of stone laid, then a course of strong balk or timber, and so on up to the full height of the structure, the wood binding the masonry together.

On the expenses Clarke draws a careful distinction from the parallel records. Cyrus had ordered timber to be cut at Lebanon and conveyed down to Joppa at his own charge; but it does not appear, the wesleyan-arminian Clarke argues, that the crown furnished the general cost of the building, for the Jews themselves contributed toward that. What the king did provide from his revenue, as the following verses show, were the sacrifices and offerings for the temple service. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, expounding the decree as a whole, take the clause as Cyrus's pledge that the cost of the work should be met from the royal house.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the warrant with an eye to its aftermath. Here, he says, is a warrant for the taking of the building's expenses out of the king's revenue; yet we do not find that the Jews ever received what was thus ordered them, the face of things at court being soon changed after Cyrus. The good intention of the first decree was, in the event, not fully executed, and the work had languished — until Darius, finding the old order, revived and enforced it.

The witnesses do not contend; they fit the pieces together into a single picture. A generous edict had provided both for the fabric of the house and for its worship, dressing stone with timber and charging the treasury with the bill; but the shifting of imperial favour had left much of that provision on paper only, so that the returned exiles bore no small part of the burden themselves. The verse thus stands as both a memorial of royal liberality and a quiet reminder that the promises of princes are not always performed, and that the completion of God's house would owe as much to the perseverance of his people as to the bounty of a king.
5:
The final clause of Cyrus's edict — that the golden and silver vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had carried from the temple be restored, every one to its place — turns the witnesses to the sacred plate and the long story of its captivity and return. The reformed John Gill notes that this provision confirms the very thing the Jews had told Tatnai in their defence, that Cyrus had commanded the restoration of the vessels; the decree now unearthed vindicates their word. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the grammar of the command, reading the singular 'let it go to its place' as distributive — each several vessel to its own appointed station — and referring the matter back to the first restoration recorded at Ezra 1:7 and the plea of Ezra 5:14.

Charles Ellicott presses the theological weight of the return. These were the very vessels that Belshazzar had profaned at his feast, drinking wine from the holy cups before the gods of gold and silver; their restoration to the sanctuary was thus, he says, an expiation of that desecration recorded in Daniel 5:2-3. And he marks the emphatic style of the decree, every word weighty, the phrase 'the house of God' repeated twice over, as though to stamp the sacredness of the charge upon the officers who must execute it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry rounds out the sense of the warrant. It is, he says, an order for the restoring of the vessels and utensils of the temple which Nebuchadnezzar had taken away, with the direction that the priests, the Lord's ministers, should return them all to their proper places in the house of God. Those who had thought to control the priests must now, in this matter, be at their command.

The witnesses converge on the quiet justice of it. Vessels torn from the temple by a conqueror, hoarded in Babylon, and at last profaned by a drunken king on the night his kingdom fell, are by imperial decree to be gathered up and carried home, set once more where they had stood before the exile. The God who had given them into captivity now brings them back, and the very cups whose profanation had spelled Babylon's doom become the furniture of a restored worship — a token that what the enemies of God's house had seized and defiled, he would reclaim and sanctify again. That the pagan decree should trouble itself to name and number the sacred plate, and to insist that each piece return to its own place, the witnesses take as a further mark of the strange care that Providence had laid upon a heathen court for the ordering of Israel's sanctuary.
6:
With the edict of Cyrus verified, the record turns to Darius's own answer, and the witnesses mark the abruptness with which the king rounds on the very officials who had lodged the complaint. The reformed John Gill identifies the parties: Tatnai, governor on the far side of the Euphrates toward the land of Israel — a man whom Josephus styles the master of the horse — with Shetharboznai and their companions. Charles Ellicott notes the sudden shift of voice: here the text passes without warning into the decree of Darius itself, whose terms were either framed with Jewish help or freely rendered by the historian into the national phraseology; and the command 'be ye far from thence' he reads as an order to keep wholly aloof from any kind of interference.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the substance of what follows. Acting on the discovered edict, Darius warned the governor and the royal officers on this side of the river not to hinder the building of the house of God at Jerusalem, but rather to promote it, furnishing what was needed and paying the costs out of the royal revenue to the elders of the Jews. Adam Clarke puts the charge plainly: do not interrupt the Jews in their building, but on the contrary further them to the utmost of your power.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the very form of the words a knowledge of the officers' hearts. The manner of the expression, he observes, intimates that Darius knew they had a mind to hinder the work: 'Be ye far hence; let the work of this house of God alone.' Thus, he says, was the wrath of the enemy made to praise God, and the remainder of that wrath he did restrain.

The witnesses do not divide. Together they catch the wonder of the reversal: the men who had ridden out to arrest the building, and who had written to the throne in hope of an order to suppress it, receive instead a royal command to stand back and let it proceed. The instrument the adversaries had chosen for the Jews' undoing becomes, in the hand of God, the guarantee of their protection; and the governor beyond the river, so lately a threat, is bound by his own sovereign to keep his distance from the work he had meant to stop. The very abruptness Ellicott noticed — the decree breaking in without preamble — measures how completely the king's mind had been changed, so that the answer to the officers' letter reads less as a reply than as a rebuke, ordering the accusers to become, at their own charge, the protectors of the accused.
7:
The heart of the royal order — 'let the work of this house of God alone' — the witnesses read as a full and deliberate withdrawal of every hindrance, and as a positive commission to the Jewish leaders to build. The reformed John Gill takes the words as a plain permission: suffer them to go on, and do not hinder them; and he detects in the emphatic phrasing a hint that Darius had been told, or suspected, that his officers were inclined to molest the builders, or that others were stirring them up to it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the sense of the verb — to leave a thing alone, to let it go forward without hindrance — and note that the decree names its builders: the governor of the Jews, whether Sheshbazzar or Zerubbabel, together with the elders, are to raise this house of God in its place, the second clause laying a special emphasis upon the elders.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the force of the command into his running account of Darius's decree, which he finds explicit and satisfactory: the king forbids his officers to do anything in opposition to the building, and the very manner of his speech betrays that he knew they had a mind to hinder it. What Cyrus had permitted and the adversaries had obstructed, Darius now not merely permits but requires; the work is placed under the protection of the crown, and the men who would have stopped it are ordered to let it stand.

The witnesses do not contend. They agree that the verse marks the decisive turn from the long paralysis that opposition had imposed since the reign of the earlier kings, when the work was made to cease by force at Ezra 4:23. Now the same imperial machinery that had once enforced the halt is set to secure the resumption. The elders of the Jews, who had ventured to build on the strength of prophetic encouragement even while the appeal to Darius was pending, are vindicated: their boldness proves to have been faith, not presumption, for the king's answer confirms the very work they had dared to continue. The decree does not create their right to build; it recognizes and defends a right that rested, all along, on the commandment of the God of Israel and the ancient grant of Cyrus. Gill's suspicion that some had been stirring up the officers to molest the builders only deepens the mercy of the reversal: where a whisper of opposition might once have sufficed to halt the work, now the plain word of the king places it beyond the reach of every local malice, and bids the elders build on unafraid.
8:
Darius now moves from mere permission to positive patronage — 'of the king's goods, even of the tribute beyond the river, forthwith let expences be given unto these men' — and the witnesses weigh both the generosity and its source. The reformed John Gill treats this as an additional decree, going beyond Cyrus in what it grants and framed as an encouragement to press the work forward; though he records the view of Josephus, that all of this was really no more than a confirmation of what Cyrus had already ordained. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch expound the mechanism: out of the royal moneys, specifically the custom or tribute levied on the province beyond the Euphrates, the cost of the building is to be paid to the elders punctually and in full, so that the work suffer no cessation — the Vulgate rightly catching the sense, that the building be not impeded.

Charles Ellicott sharpens the fiscal point: the king says, in effect, 'I also make my decree,' and the sums for the temple are to be deducted from the very tribute that the province would otherwise have remitted to Persia. It is not from some separate bounty but from the imperial revenue itself, the taxes of the region, that the house of God is to be financed — the empire, in a sense, paying for the sanctuary of a subject people.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fills in the astonishment of it. Darius orders his own officers, out of his revenue, to assist the builders with money for carrying on the work, herein following the example Cyrus had set; and it was a new thing indeed, Henry marvels, for God's priests to have such an interest in the public money, and for those who had thought to control the work to be, in this very matter, at the builders' command.

The witnesses do not divide. They see one hand behind the arrangement. The tribute wrung from the lands beyond the river, which the adversaries no doubt hoped to see turned against the Jews, is instead diverted to their aid; the wealth of the empire is made to serve the worship of the God of heaven. What had begun as an accusation designed to cut off the building has ended in a standing charge upon the royal treasury for its completion — the clearest proof yet that when God's time to favour his church is come, he can make even a heathen exchequer the purse of his house.
9:
The decree descends to particulars, itemizing what the temple will need for its daily worship — young bullocks, rams, and lambs for the burnt offerings, with wheat, salt, wine, and oil — to be furnished at the priests' direction, day by day without fail; and the witnesses admire the exactness of a pagan king's provision for a worship not his own. The reformed John Gill notes only that all these were the appointed materials of the burnt offering. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch dwell on the phrase 'day by day without fail,' reading it as a guarantee that the supply should never lapse, so that the service of God might be maintained continually and the priests never be left wanting.

Charles Ellicott is struck by the accuracy of the list. It is, he says, a precise account of the provision required for the sacrifices and the meat-offerings of the daily service, and how precise will appear to anyone who consults the ritual law of Exodus 29 and Leviticus 2; the very word rendered 'appointment' means simply the direction or command of the priests, whose office it was to prescribe what the altar required. Such correspondence with the Mosaic prescriptions persuades Ellicott that the decree was drawn up under good instruction, by someone who knew the Jewish ritual from within.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the daily allowance as a mark of the king's earnestness. Darius ordered that they should be supplied with everything they wanted, both for burnt-offerings and for meat-offerings; he was content that it should be a standing charge upon his revenue, and commanded it to be paid every day, and this without fail.

The witnesses converge on the marvel of the thing. A Persian monarch, no worshipper of Israel's God, undertakes to keep the fire burning on a foreign altar, and to see that neither bullock nor lamb, neither grain nor salt nor wine nor oil, should ever be lacking for it. The care that Israel's own kings had too often neglected is here assumed by a stranger, at the prompting of the God who was inclining the heart of the empire toward his house — so that the very sacrifices of Jerusalem were secured, morning and evening, by the word of Darius and the tribute of Persia. And the daily, unfailing character of the supply is not lost on them: a worship that must be renewed every morning is underwritten by a standing charge that may not lapse, so that the continual burnt offering, the very emblem of Israel's unbroken communion with God, rests no longer on the fitful zeal of her own princes but on the firm decree of a foreign king whom God had made its guardian.
10:
The king now names his own motive — that the priests may offer sacrifices of sweet savour to the God of heaven, and pray for the life of the king and of his sons — and the witnesses probe both the piety and the policy in it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain that the sacrifices are those 'well-pleasing' to God, and that Darius here treads in the footsteps of Cyrus, who had owned the God of Israel as the God of heaven who gave him his kingdoms, as recorded at Ezra 1:2. Such acknowledgment, they observe, the Persian kings could make without renouncing their own polytheism; they might honour Jahve as the mightiest God of heaven and still keep the gods of their fathers, and Darius plainly desired that the blessing of this God should rest upon himself and his dynasty.

Charles Ellicott finds two ends answered in the clause: the God of heaven is to be honoured, and the house of Darius interceded for by the Jews, much as Jeremiah had bidden the exiles pray for the peace of the city of their captivity in Jeremiah 29:7. He renders 'sweet savours' by the word for incense that recurs at Daniel 2:46, and finds in the linking of sacrifice with prayer a further sign of the good instruction under which the decree was framed.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the striking fact that even a heathen believed the offerings and prayers made on his behalf to the God of the Jews would avail him; and he notes how this persuasion has moved more than one state to tolerate a religion not its own, that the commonwealth might have the benefit of its people's prayers. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the honours Darius here pays: to Israel's God, whom he calls again and again the God of heaven; to God's ministers, whose direction his commissioners must follow; and to prayer, for he knew the Jews were a praying people to whom God was nigh, and he was wise enough to court their intercession. It is the duty of God's people, Henry adds, to pray for those in authority, and the wisdom of princes to desire and engage such prayers, since it is desirable to have them for us and dreadful to have them against us.

The witnesses do not divide. They see a king who, whether from genuine reverence or shrewd statecraft or both, has bound his throne to the altar of Jerusalem, and made the prosperity of his dynasty hang, in part, upon the prayers of the people his predecessors had carried captive.
11:
The decree arms itself with a fearful sanction — whoever alters this word, let timber be pulled from his house, and let him be hanged upon it, and his house be made a dunghill — and the witnesses examine both the crime and the mode of its punishment. The reformed John Gill glosses 'alter this word' as to act contrary to the command, to change or revoke as much as in one lies. Charles Ellicott sharpens it: the phrase means to violate the command, since the literal altering of a royal decree was in Persia a thing unheard of; and the penalty he takes with the plainest severity, for 'hanged' is properly 'crucified.'

On the manner of execution the grammatical-historical witnesses supply the grim realia. Keil and Delitzsch describe a beam torn from the offender's own house and set upright, on which he was to be fastened and lifted up; and they note that this form of capital punishment was customary among the Assyrians and the ancient Persians, the Assyrians commonly impaling the condemned upon a sharp stake, as the monuments unearthed at Nineveh depict, and as Herodotus records that Darius himself once impaled his enemies by the thousand. Here a genuine difference of detail opens between the witnesses. Ellicott distinguishes the practices: among the Persians crucifixion was generally the nailing of a body to a cross after the head had been struck off, while among the Assyrians it was transfixion or impalement; and he insists that the 'setting up' in the verse refers to the man, not to the beam. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke leaves the choice open — whether hanging, gibbeting, or empaling is meant is not quite clear — but inclines to empalement, the thrusting of a sharp stake through the body, or else hanging.

On the ruin of the house the witnesses agree. To make it a dunghill, Clarke explains, is to reduce it to ruins, never again to be used but for the vilest and most unclean purposes; the man's dwelling, which furnished the instrument of his death, is left a monument of shame.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sums the sanction in a homely phrase: the transgressor is to be hanged, as we say, before his own door, upon a beam of his own house, and, as an execrable man, his house made a dunghill. The witnesses do not soften the horror; they let it stand as the measure of how earnestly Darius meant his decree to be obeyed, that the building of God's house should be secured, if need be, by the terror of the gallows.
12:
The king ends his decree by invoking a power higher than his own — 'the God that hath caused his name to dwell there destroy all kings and people that shall put to their hand to alter and to destroy this house' — and the witnesses hear in the words a distinctly Israelite theology on a Persian tongue. The reformed John Gill observes that Darius speaks of a God who not only is called upon there and owns the place by his name, but who grants his presence and causes his divine Majesty to dwell there, as in Solomon's temple — a knowledge of Israel's God the king had somehow come by. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch press the point: the very phrase 'the God who has caused his name to dwell there' is unmistakably biblical, echoing the language of Deuteronomy 12:11 and the prophets, and must have come from the Jewish historian's own pen; yet the substance — the wish that God himself would destroy any who should injure his temple — recalls the close of the great Bisitun inscription, where Darius calls down the judgments of Ahuramazda upon whoever should dare to deface his monument.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley ventures beyond the text into the long reach of the curse. Though this temple was at length most justly destroyed by the righteous hand of God, yet perhaps, he muses, the Romans, who were the instruments of that destruction, felt the effects of Darius's imprecation, for that empire sensibly declined ever after, until it was wholly destroyed. It is a bold and speculative reading, tracing the fall of Rome to the shadow of a Persian king's threat.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the invocation as the mark of a zealous heart: what Darius could not himself do for the temple's perpetual protection, he desired that God, to whom vengeance belongs, would do. Henry too weighs the paradox that the house thus solemnly guarded was in the end destroyed, and shares Wesley's surmise that the Roman instruments of that ruin may have felt the curse in their empire's decline.

The witnesses converge on the wonder of the confession. A heathen monarch closes his edict not with his own name only — 'I Darius have made a decree; let it be done with speed' — but with an appeal to the God of Israel as the true avenger of his house, thereby lending the whole authority of Persia to the God of heaven, and setting the sanctuary of Jerusalem under a double guard, imperial and divine.
13:
The narrative now watches the royal word take effect, and the witnesses mark how swiftly the officers who had opposed the work turn to forwarding it. The reformed John Gill notes simply that Tatnai, Shetharboznai, and their companions, having received and read the king's letter, did as they were bidden. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch stress the diligence: because Darius the king had sent his answer — the very decree whose terms have just been rehearsed — they executed his commands speedily and to the letter.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on the reversal with evident relish. Here, he says, are the Jews' enemies made their friends. When they received this order from the king, they came with as much haste to encourage and assist the work as their predecessors had come to put a stop to it when the building was forced to cease by royal command in Ezra 4:23. What the king ordered, they did; and because they would not be thought to do it grudgingly, they did it speedily. The king's own moderation, Henry observes, made them — contrary to their own inclination — moderate too; men who had ridden to Jerusalem to interrogate and obstruct now bent the same energy to the very cause they had meant to crush.

The witnesses do not divide, and the lesson they draw is of a piece with the whole chapter. The same hands are set to a wholly opposite work, not by any change of heart in the men themselves, but by the turning of a king's decree, which is itself the turning of a king's heart in the hand of God. Tatnai's obedience is prompt because disobedience to Darius was perilous; but the deeper cause lies behind the throne, in the providence that had inclined Darius to favour the Jews and had thereby disarmed their adversaries. So the opposition that had dogged the building from its first foundation is not merely lifted but converted into aid, and the officers of the empire become, in spite of themselves, the servants of the God of Israel — a fresh proof that when the Lord will have his house built, even its enemies must lend their hands to the raising of it. Henry lets the word 'speedily' carry its own sting of irony: the haste with which Tatnai now obeys matches, and answers, the haste with which his predecessors had earlier run to Jerusalem to stop the work by force. The same eagerness that had served malice is bent to service; and the swiftness that Keil and Delitzsch commend as diligence is, in Henry's reading, the plainest sign that a higher hand than the king's had turned the whole current of the officers' will.
14:
The building at last goes forward to completion, and the witnesses gather around the several agents the verse names — the elders, the prophets, and the succession of Persian kings — all of them, in the end, subordinate to one commanding will. The reformed John Gill notes plainly that the elders of the Jews went on with the work. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the theological nerve of the verse from the phrase 'through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah': this is a seasonable intimation, he says, that the great and unexpected success was not to be ascribed to chance, nor to the kindness or good humour of Darius, but to God alone, who by his prophets had required and encouraged the work, and by his mighty power had disposed the king's heart to such noble purposes.

The naming of the kings — Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes — raises a difficulty the grammatical-historical witnesses take pains to resolve. Keil and Delitzsch note that Artaxerxes cannot here be a predecessor of Darius, and can only be Artaxerxes Longimanus, who reigned long after the temple was finished; his name is joined to the others because, by his later edict at Ezra 7, he too furthered the work of God's house. Charles Ellicott agrees, observing that this verse gathers up all the agents of the great enterprise from Cyrus to Artaxerxes, and that Artaxerxes alone is styled 'king of Persia,' which shows that Ezra is writing in his reign and adds his name to the original record. Adam Clarke lays out the chronology of the reigns — Cyrus first giving the order, Darius Hystaspes confirming it, and Artaxerxes Longimanus afterward sending Ezra and then permitting Nehemiah — a recapitulation of all the sovereigns who favoured the Jews after the captivity.

Yet Ellicott is careful to add that all of it is from the God of Israel, whose commandment Cyrus and every other king did but fulfil. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the same order of causes: the elders built cheerfully, bound to it by the commandment of the God of Israel, shamed into diligence by the zeal of heathen kings, and encouraged by the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah; and in some four years' time the work was brought to perfection. 'As for God, his work is perfect,' Henry adds, turning the finished temple into a figure of that spiritual house, long in the building, which shall be completed at last when the whole mystical body is complete.

The witnesses do not divide. Prophets urge, kings decree, elders labour; but the verse subordinates them all to the commandment of the God of Israel, who is the true builder of his own house.
15:
The exact dating of the temple's completion — the third day of the month Adar, in the sixth year of Darius — draws the witnesses to fix the moment with care and to measure the long span it closes. The reformed John Gill identifies Adar as the twelfth month, answering to part of February and part of March. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch parse the verb 'was finished' as a causative form meaning to bring a thing to its end; and they note that the apocryphal Esdras gives the twenty-third day rather than the third, a variant some have wished to prefer, though the Hebrew text reads the third.

Adam Clarke sets the completion in his chronological scheme: the sixth year of Darius fell about the year of the world 3489, some twenty years after the foundation had been laid by Zerubbabel under Cyrus. Charles Ellicott dates it with still greater precision to the third day of the last month of the ecclesiastical year, in the winter of 516 to 515 before Christ. Reckoning from the resumption of the work, whose exact date Haggai supplies at Haggai 1:15, he counts the interval at four years, five months, and ten days; but reckoning from the first laying of the foundation at Ezra 3:10, no less than twenty-one years had elapsed.

The witnesses do not divide over the substance; their small disagreements concern only the day of the month and the precise arithmetic of the years. What they agree in feeling is the weight of the moment. A work begun amid the tears and shoutings of the first returning exiles, interrupted by opposition, discouraged by poverty, and halted for years together, is at last carried through to its end, and the historian is careful to nail the date, that later generations might know exactly when the house of God stood finished. The two decades and more of delay are gathered up into a single dated line — a reminder that God's purposes, though long in ripening, come at the appointed season to their fruit, and that the very slowness of the building only magnifies the faithfulness that at length completed it, according to the word of the prophets and the commandment of the King of kings. Ellicott's two reckonings — four years and some months from the day the discouraged builders resumed their labour, one-and-twenty years from the day the first stone was laid — set the brevity of the final push against the long weariness that went before, so that the whole history of the second temple is folded into this one dated verse: a great work begun in hope, stalled in fear, and finished at last in the fulness of God's time.
16:
With the house finished, the returned people keep its dedication, and the witnesses attend to the company gathered and the sacrifices they bring. The reformed John Gill takes 'the children of Israel' to include such of the ten tribes as had remained in the land or come back with the returning Jews, so that the dedication was not of Judah only. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the Aramaic idiom for keeping a dedication and set out the offerings: a hundred bullocks, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs for burnt offerings, and twelve he-goats as a sin offering for all Israel, according to the number of the tribes — for the temple was intended for the entire covenant people, whose return, according to the prophets, was still hoped for, as in the visions of Ezekiel 37:15 and the promise of Jeremiah 31:27.

Charles Ellicott notes how fitting the title 'children of the captivity' is at this moment, standing as it does beside the fuller name 'all Israel' that soon follows: the little remnant of the exile keeps a feast for the whole people of the twelve tribes. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the mingled dignity and poverty of the assembly. The persons employed were not the priests and Levites only, but the children of Israel, some of every tribe, though Judah and Benjamin were the chief, together with the rest of the children of the captivity — a phrase in which Henry hears both the presence of proselytes from other nations and the humbled condition of a people who, once 'the children of Israel,' are now 'the children of the captivity,' a remnant only, according to the prophecy of Shear-jashub, 'the remnant shall return,' in Isaiah 7:3.

The witnesses do not divide. They read the dedication as a small but wholehearted act of a chastened nation. The offerings are modest beside the thousands Solomon had slain at the first dedication, yet they are brought with joy; and the twelve he-goats, one for every tribe, confess that this house belongs not to the returned fragment alone but to the whole covenant people, scattered and diminished though they are. The remnant keeps the feast in hope, laying its poverty upon the altar and looking, over the ruins of the exile, toward the fuller restoration the prophets had promised — a dedication whose true grandeur lay not in the number of its victims but in the faith and gladness with which they were offered.
17:
The tally of the dedication offerings — a hundred bullocks, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and twelve he-goats for a sin offering — draws the witnesses to both the scale of the sacrifice and its representative meaning. The reformed John Gill calls these hecatombs, the grand sacrifices reckoned magnificent even among the heathen, of which Homer sometimes speaks; some were burnt offerings and some peace offerings, offered in thankfulness for the finished house, and of the peace offerings the worshippers would feast their own portion with great gladness of heart.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes on the twelve he-goats: this, he says, was a sin offering for every tribe, one for each. Charles Ellicott presses the significance of that number. The people are here no longer merely 'Judah' or 'Judah and Benjamin' but 'all Israel'; and though on the Day of Atonement, at the new moons, and at the great feasts a single kid was the appointed sin offering for the whole people, only here is one offered for each several tribe — a deliberate confession that the house and its atonement belonged to the entire nation of the twelve.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the offerings against Solomon's and finds them small in number but not in acceptance. They were not to be compared with the thousands the first temple had seen, yet being according to the people's present ability they were accepted; for after a great trial of affliction, their deep poverty had abounded to the riches of their liberality, as Paul says of the Macedonians in 2 Corinthians 8:2, so that these hundreds were more to them than Solomon's thousands were to him. And Henry marks the wisdom of the sin offering: by twelve he-goats, one for every tribe, they made atonement for their sins, which they rightly judged necessary if their service was to be accepted, so that iniquity being taken away might not prove a worm at the root of their present comforts.

The witnesses do not divide. They see in the dedication a worship poor in its resources but rich in its intention, and above all penitent: before the burnt offerings could ascend as sweet savour, atonement must be made, tribe by tribe, for the sin of a people newly restored. The returned remnant does not presume upon its deliverance but confesses its guilt, and lays a sin offering for all Israel upon the altar of the house it has just raised.
18:
With the house dedicated, the people order its ministry, setting the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their courses for the service of God at Jerusalem, as it is written in the book of Moses; and the witnesses attend to this founding of an ordered worship. The reformed John Gill notes simply that all were placed in their proper classes and courses, to do the work of the temple each in his turn. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain that the priests and Levites were appointed by their classes and divisions, that each course might henceforth serve in its own week, after the pattern set in 2 Chronicles 23:4 and 2 Kings 11:9; and they observe that with this verse the long Aramaic section of the book comes to its close — a point Adam Clarke likewise marks.

Charles Ellicott adds a careful qualification. The book of Moses gave only the general arrangements; the twenty-four courses themselves were of David's institution; and the restoration now made must have been imperfect, since neither were the twenty-four priestly courses complete nor were the Levites present in their full number, so many having failed to return from exile. The order re-established was thus a diminished echo of the fuller service of former days.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the pastoral sense of the arrangement. When they had dedicated the house, they settled the household; for small comfort could they have taken in the temple without the temple service, and so they set the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their courses, making the book of Moses their rule and keeping their eye upon it in the whole establishment. Though the service could not now be performed with the pomp and plenty of Solomon's day, Henry observes, it was perhaps performed with as much purity and as close an adherence to the divine institution as ever — and there is, he says, no beauty like the beauty of holiness.

The witnesses do not divide. They see a people who, having built and dedicated the house, take care that it shall not stand empty, but be filled with the appointed worship of God, ordered exactly by the ancient rule. What their poverty could not supply in splendour they made up in fidelity; and the closing of the Aramaic record on this note of settled, Mosaic order signals that the restoration is not merely of a building but of a worship, established to endure.
19:
The narrative, returning here to the Hebrew tongue, records the first great festival kept in the finished house — the children of the captivity keeping the passover on the fourteenth day of the first month — and the witnesses mark both the timing and the fitness of the feast. The reformed John Gill notes that this was the month Nisan, or Abib, falling in the very month after the temple was completed, and that the passover was kept at the exact time the law commanded. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the celebration as a historical testimony that the worship of God, with its appointed festivals, was now regularly carried on in the new temple; the feast, they observe, followed only a few weeks after the dedication.

Charles Ellicott hears in the moment a rich significance. Recording this special passover, kept after the precedent of Hezekiah and Josiah, Ezra returns to the Hebrew language of his people; and the occasion was, as it were, a renewal of the redemption from Egypt, for another wilderness had now been passed and another bondage brought to an end.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the same likeness. Now that they were newly delivered out of their bondage in Babylon, it was seasonable to commemorate their deliverance out of their bondage in Egypt; fresh mercies, he says, should ever put us in mind of former mercies. They had, he supposes, kept the passover after a sort every year since their return, having an altar and a tabernacle; but liable to disturbance from their enemies, straitened for room, and lacking convenience, they could not keep it with due solemnity until the temple was built. Now at last they made a joyful festival of it, falling as it did in the month after the house was finished and dedicated.

The witnesses do not divide. Together they see the passover as the natural first act of a restored worship, and as a parable of the whole return. A people just brought up out of captivity keep the feast that memorializes their fathers' coming up out of Egypt, and find in the ancient deliverance the pattern of their own. The redemption from Babylon is read through the redemption from Egypt; the two exoduses answer one another across the centuries, and the passover kept in the new temple binds the latest mercy of God to the first, confessing one hand behind them both.
20:
The record pauses over the purity of the ministers who slew the passover — the priests and the Levites purified together, all of them pure — and the witnesses find in that unanimous cleansing a mark of the celebration's excellence. The reformed John Gill renders the phrase 'as one man': all were purified together, of one mind to sanctify themselves, and did it with such dispatch that they were all, to a man, pure — more generally prepared for the service, he notes, than had been the case even in the days of Hezekiah. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm that the priests and Levites had purified themselves without exception, so that being all clean they were fit to kill the passover for the whole assembly — for the laity returned from exile, for their brethren the priests, and for themselves.

Charles Ellicott presses the grammar toward the same sense, translating against the received accentuation: 'the priests were purified; and the Levites were purified as one man: all were pure; and killed.' In this the present Levitical purity of both orders surpassed that of Hezekiah's celebration, where many of the priests had been found unsanctified, as the Chronicler records at 2 Chronicles 29:34 and 2 Chronicles 30:3; and Ellicott notes that it had by now become the practice for the Levites to slaughter all the paschal lambs. Adam Clarke adds that they were all ready together at the one time, with no need of that second passover which the law had appointed for such as were accidentally defiled or at a distance from the sanctuary.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the lesson. In Hezekiah's time many of the priests had lain under blame for not purifying themselves; but now it is recorded to their praise that they were purified together, as one man, unanimous both in their resolution and in their endeavour to be clean for the solemnity. The purity of ministers, Henry observes, adds much to the beauty of their ministrations, and so does their unity.

The witnesses do not divide. They see in this general sanctification a happy contrast to earlier and more careless days, and a fitting preparation for the feast: the men who must handle the blood of the passover are themselves first cleansed, and cleansed together, that nothing in the ministers might mar the worship of a people newly restored to their God. Clarke's small observation only sharpens the point: because all were ready and clean at the one appointed time, there was no need of that later, second passover which the law had provided for the accidentally defiled — the whole company kept the feast at its proper season, in a purity so complete that the very exception the law allowed was not required of them.
21:
The passover is eaten not only by the returned exiles but by 'all such as had separated themselves unto them from the filthiness of the heathen of the land, to seek the LORD God of Israel'; and over the identity of these separated ones the witnesses genuinely divide. The reformed John Gill takes the eaters to be the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, with some of the ten tribes mingled among them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the separated ones as proselytes — heathen who had embraced the Jewish religion, having mingled with the Jews during the captivity; the poor captives, he says, had so lived out the principles of their faith that the heathen saw it and were drawn to walk in the light of the Lord with them, a proof of how persuasive a good example is when founded on pure principle.

Charles Ellicott flatly contradicts this reading. The verse does not mean proselytes from the heathen at all, he argues, but the remnant of the Jews left in the land, who had consorted with the foreign populations the conquerors had introduced, and who now separated themselves from that defilement to seek the God of Israel — their intermarriages and other acts of conformity being a matter referred to again and again throughout Ezra and Nehemiah. So the debate is drawn: were the newcomers to the feast Gentile converts won by the exiles' witness, or lapsed Israelites of the land purifying themselves from heathen entanglements? John Wesley, for his part, takes 'the children of Israel' broadly, as probably including some out of each of the twelve tribes.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the separation without pressing the disputed point: those who parted from the uncleanness of the heathen races of the country did so to seek Jahve the God of Israel, the very language of covenant devotion. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, siding with the reading of converts, dwells on the pattern of true religion the verse displays: they separated themselves from the filthiness of sin and from fellowship with sinners, joined themselves to the Israel of God in conformity and communion, and set themselves to seek the God of Israel; and those who do so in sincerity, though strangers and foreigners, are welcome to the gospel feast as fellow-citizens with the saints and of the household of God.

The witnesses agree, whatever their difference over the persons, upon the principle. The passover is open to all who will renounce the pollutions of the heathen and seek the LORD; the door of the covenant stands ajar for every sincere seeker, native or stranger, who separates himself from uncleanness to worship the God of Israel.
22:
The chapter closes on a week of gladness — the feast of unleavened bread kept seven days with joy, 'for the LORD had made them joyful, and turned the heart of the king of Assyria unto them' — and the witnesses dwell on the source of the joy and on the puzzle of that royal title. The reformed John Gill notes only that this feast immediately followed the passover, as the law prescribed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain that it was the Lord who had made them joyful, and made them so by turning the king's heart toward them, strengthening their hands for the work of his house; and they identify the 'king of Assyria' as the Persian Darius, so styled because he ruled the former realm of Assyria.

On that title the witnesses are of one mind. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, following Calmet, holds that 'king of Assyria' stands here for the king of Persia, since Cyrus and his successors had inherited all the rights and estates of the ancient Assyrian kings; and he adds a touch of history, that Darius had married two daughters of Cyrus, and so was the readier to confirm his father-in-law's edict in favour of the Jews. Charles Ellicott reads the name as a deliberate remembrancer, the king of Persia called 'king of Assyria' to recall the oppression the people had suffered under his forerunners. John Wesley presses the same point with feeling: he is called king of Assyria emphatically, to note the great power and goodness of God in turning the hearts of these mighty monarchs, whose predecessors had been the chief persecutors and oppressors of God's people.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers on the joy itself. The Lord had given them both cause to rejoice and hearts to rejoice, for he is the fountain whence all the streams of true joy flow; and Henry recalls that it was now some twenty years since the foundation had been laid, so that the old men who had wept at the memory of the first temple were mostly dead, and no tears were now mingled with the people's gladness. The particular occasion of their joy was that God had turned the heart of the emperor to strengthen their hands; and when those we feared would be against us prove to be for us, Henry says, we may take it as a token for good that our ways please the Lord, according to the promise of Proverbs 16:7.

The witnesses do not divide. They end the chapter where it began, in the sovereignty of God over the hearts of kings: the same power that had moved Darius to search the archives now fills a restored people with gladness, having turned an oppressor's throne into a patron of his house.
